messages.text: I have a 10x dataset of about 40k cells from mouse bone marrow, sorted for stem and progenitor populations. I want to order the cells along pseudotime from the most primitive stem cells toward erythroid and myeloid states. I tried diffusion pseudotime with a root cell I picked by hand from the stem cluster, but I'm nervous the ordering is very sensitive to which root I pick. How do people usually handle that?

Root sensitivity is a common concern. A few practical steps: choose the root using a marker-based score rather than a single hand-picked cell, for example the cell with the highest stemness signature, or the extreme of the first diffusion component within the stem cluster. Then rerun with several candidate roots from that cluster and check the rank correlation of the resulting orderings. If correlations are high, say above 0.9, your ordering is robust. Also check the number of neighbours and diffusion components, since those affect pseudotime more than people expect.

Good idea, I'll do the multiple-roots check. Another thing: my erythroid cells look nicely ordered but the myeloid side is a mess, with neutrophil and monocyte precursors mixed together in pseudotime. I suspect a single linear ordering just doesn't make sense once you pass the point where they diverge. Should I be computing the ordering separately per lineage?

Your suspicion is probably right. A single pseudotime value can't represent divergent paths; cells at the same pseudotime on different branches look 'mixed' in a one-dimensional view. Methods like Slingshot or Palantir fit separate curves or compute branch probabilities, giving each cell a pseudotime per lineage plus a weight for how committed it is. Alternatively, subset to each myeloid branch after identifying the split and order those cells separately. Checking known markers along each branch, like Elane for neutrophils and Irf8 for monocytes, will help confirm the ordering is biologically sensible.

I'm trying to combine my own bone marrow single-cell data with two public datasets from other labs. Before correction the cells cluster almost perfectly by dataset, which is obviously technical. I ran Harmony and it looks mixed now, but I'm worried I've over-corrected and erased real biological differences, since one public dataset is from older mice. How do I tell good integration from over-integration?

That's the central tension in integration. Use metrics on both sides: batch mixing scores like kBET or iLISI tell you whether batches mix, while biological conservation metrics like cell-type ARI or cLISI tell you whether known cell types stay separated. Benchmarking frameworks report both together. For your age concern, a useful check is to look for differential expression of known age-associated genes within matched cell types after integration; if those signals vanish, you've likely over-corrected. Note that Harmony corrects the embedding, not the counts, so DE on raw counts with batch as a covariate is still possible.

That's helpful, I didn't realise Harmony only touches the embedding. I think I'll compare Harmony with scVI too, since scVI lets me include age as a separate covariate. Do you think it's legitimate to include age as a biological covariate while correcting for lab, given that age and lab are partly confounded in my design?

It's legitimate only to the extent the design allows it. If every old-mouse sample comes from one lab, lab and age are perfectly confounded and no method can separate them; the model will attribute the difference to whichever variable you tell it is technical. If there's partial overlap, for example your own data includes some older animals, scVI can use that overlap to estimate both effects. I'd make that limitation explicit and check results on the overlapping samples alone as a sanity check.

Totally different topic from my usual work. A friend is building a small quadrotor drone and asked me about trajectory optimisation, since I do numerical stuff. From what I've read, minimum-snap polynomial trajectories are the standard. Why snap specifically, the fourth derivative of position? It seems arbitrary to me, and I'm not sure it's better than just minimising time or energy.

It's less arbitrary than it looks. Quadrotors are differentially flat: position and yaw determine the full state and inputs. Thrust relates to acceleration, and the body angular rates relate to jerk, so angular acceleration, which is directly tied to motor torques, relates to snap. Minimising snap therefore smooths the motor commands, reducing abrupt rotor speed changes. It also turns into a convenient quadratic program over polynomial coefficients. Minimum-time formulations are popular for racing, but they push actuators to saturation and are nonconvex, so they're harder to solve reliably.

Oh, the differential flatness part makes it click. So snap is basically a proxy for how hard the motors are working. For a hobby drone that just needs to fly smoothly between waypoints, I'm guessing minimum-snap is plenty and the time allocation between segments is the harder part. Is that right?

Yes, that's a good summary. For smooth waypoint flight minimum snap works well, and segment time allocation is indeed the trickier part, since bad allocations can make polynomials overshoot or violate velocity limits. Common approaches include heuristic allocation from distance and maximum speed, then iteratively scaling times until constraints are satisfied, or optimising times by gradient descent on total cost. Libraries for minimum-snap generation often include such routines, so your friend may not need to implement it from scratch.

chats.title: Can I trust RNA velocity arrows?

messages.text: I ran scVelo on my hematopoiesis data and most of the velocity arrows point from stem cells toward erythroid cells, which is what I expect. But a chunk of the megakaryocyte progenitors have arrows pointing backwards, toward the stem cluster. I'm not sure if that's real biology or the method breaking. How much should I trust the direction of these arrows for saying which way differentiation goes?

Some caution is warranted. RNA velocity relies on the ratio of unspliced to spliced reads and assumes fairly constant kinetic rates across a population. In hematopoiesis, a well-known failure case involves transcriptional boosts, where a set of genes sharply increases transcription during erythroid maturation, which can flip inferred directions. Megakaryocyte and erythroid lineages share a progenitor and some of these genes. Check which genes drive the backward arrows using per-gene phase portraits; if a few genes with odd kinetics dominate, the reversal is probably an artifact.

I looked at the phase portraits and yes, a handful of genes have that weird two-arm shape. When I drop them the backward arrows mostly go away. But now I feel like I'm cherry-picking genes until I get the answer I expected. Is there a principled way to decide which genes to exclude, rather than just removing whatever disagrees with my prior?

That's a healthy worry. More principled options include: using scVelo's likelihood or fit-quality scores and excluding genes below a threshold set before looking at directions; using the differential kinetics test, which flags genes with multiple kinetic regimes across clusters; or switching to methods that allow cluster-specific rates. Report results with and without the exclusions, and state the criterion up front. Independent evidence, like metabolic labelling or lineage tracing, is the strongest way to confirm direction rather than relying on velocity alone.

Off-topic curiosity: I saw a figure of glacier surface velocity across an ice sheet made from satellite radar, and I'm curious how that works. I know InSAR measures phase differences between two radar images, but that only gives motion along the line of sight, right? How do they get full horizontal velocity fields out of that? It seems like you'd be missing a component.

You're right that a single interferogram only measures line-of-sight displacement. To recover horizontal velocity, people combine ascending and descending passes, which view the surface from different directions, and often assume flow is parallel to the surface so the vertical component can be constrained from a digital elevation model. Another approach is offset tracking, which correlates image patches between acquisitions to measure displacement in both range and azimuth directly. It's less precise than phase methods but works for fast-moving ice where interferometric phase becomes incoherent.

That makes sense, so fast outlet glaciers probably rely on offset tracking and slow interior ice on the phase method. I'd guess melting and snowfall between acquisitions also wrecks coherence. Is that why some of the velocity maps have such big gaps?

Exactly. Coherence loss from surface melting, snowfall, wind redistribution and very fast or shearing flow all cause gaps. Shorter repeat intervals help, which is why missions with frequent revisits improved coverage dramatically. Mosaics are typically built from many image pairs over a season or year to fill gaps, and some products blend radar with optical feature tracking. Your intuition about the split is right: interior ice uses phase methods for millimetre-level sensitivity, while fast margins rely on offset tracking.

chats.title: Language family trees from word lists

messages.text: I got curious about how linguists build family trees of languages. I've seen papers using Bayesian phylogenetics on lists of basic vocabulary, coding words as cognate or not. Coming from biology, I'm skeptical that borrowing between languages doesn't wreck the tree assumption, since it seems like horizontal transfer would be way more common than in genes. How do they handle it?

Borrowing is a major concern, and you're right that it's like horizontal gene transfer. Linguists mitigate it by using basic vocabulary lists, such as body parts, numbers and kinship terms, which are relatively resistant to borrowing, and by removing known loanwords during cognate coding. Some studies test how much undetected borrowing would bias results through simulations, finding that moderate borrowing mainly shortens tree branches and affects dates more than topology. Network methods like NeighborNet are also used to visualise conflicting signals rather than forcing a tree.

Interesting that borrowing hits dates more than the branching order. I'd still be suspicious of the dates in general, since the rate of word replacement surely isn't constant. Do these models still assume a strict clock like the old glottochronology did?

No, modern approaches explicitly reject glottochronology's constant rate. They use relaxed clock models, allowing rates to vary across branches, and often let different meaning classes evolve at different rates. Dates are calibrated with historically attested split times, like documented ancient languages, which act like fossil calibrations in biology. Even so, your suspicion is shared: date estimates often have wide credible intervals, and results can be sensitive to calibration choices and the cognate coding scheme.

We now have a lineage-tracing experiment in the lab where hematopoietic stem cells carry heritable DNA barcodes, and we profiled the same cells with scRNA-seq at two timepoints. I want to use the clonal information as ground truth to score how well the computational methods I've been using actually recover fate relationships. I'm not sure how to turn clone labels into a fair benchmark though.

That's a valuable setup. A common approach: use early-timepoint cells whose clones are also observed at the later timepoint, and define each early cell's 'true' fate bias as the fraction of its clonal siblings in each mature lineage at the later timepoint. Then compare that with each method's predicted fate probabilities for the same early cells, using correlation or AUROC for predicting the dominant fate. Restrict to clones with enough later cells to give a stable fraction, and report how many cells meet that criterion.

That makes sense. One complication is that only around 20 percent of barcodes get recaptured at the second timepoint, so I'm worried the evaluation set will be small and biased toward large, proliferative clones. I suspect those might be exactly the clones where prediction is easiest. Is there a way to correct for that?

Your concern about selection bias is legitimate. Options include stratifying the evaluation by clone size so you can see whether performance differs for small versus large clones, weighting each clone equally rather than each cell, and using a minimum clone size threshold but reporting results at several thresholds. You could also simulate subsampling of large clones to match the size distribution of small ones. Being explicit that the benchmark is conditional on clone recapture is important, since methods may perform worse on rarer fates.

A collaborator has a big set of fluorescence microscopy images of tissue sections and wants nuclei and cell boundaries segmented. I've only used classic watershed before. Should we go straight to a deep learning tool like Cellpose or StarDist? I'm worried about cells that are densely packed and overlapping, which is where watershed always failed for me.

For dense tissue, deep learning tools are generally a big improvement over watershed. StarDist represents nuclei as star-convex polygons, which works very well for roundish nuclei but struggles with irregular cell shapes. Cellpose predicts flow fields toward cell centres, which handles irregular and touching cells better, and has generalist pretrained models for both nuclei and whole cells. A sensible plan is to run pretrained Cellpose on a few representative images, inspect errors, and then fine-tune with a small number of manually corrected annotations if needed.

Fine-tuning with a few corrected images sounds doable. How would we know the segmentation is good enough, though? I don't want to just eyeball it. I assume we need a held-out set of hand-annotated images and some metric, but I'm not sure whether pixel accuracy is meaningful for this.

Pixel accuracy can be misleading because background dominates. Instance-level metrics are better: match predicted and true objects by intersection over union, then compute average precision across IoU thresholds, typically from 0.5 to 0.9. Also report counts of merges and splits, since those errors matter most for downstream single-cell measurements. A held-out set of a few hand-annotated images covering different tissue regions is a good start. Ideally have two people annotate a subset to estimate inter-annotator agreement as a ceiling.

Silly question while procrastinating. Could you take lineage or trajectory inference methods from biology and apply them to startups? Like treat each company as a cell, with features such as headcount, funding stage and product category, and infer how companies 'differentiate' into, say, acquired, IPO or dead. I don't actually plan to do this, I'm just wondering whether the analogy holds up at all.

It's a fun analogy and partly works. You could embed companies by feature vectors over time, build a neighbourhood graph and look for branching structure leading to terminal states like acquisition or shutdown. But there are differences: you actually have real time-series per company, so you don't need pseudotime to reconstruct order from snapshots, which is the main point of those methods in biology. Standard survival analysis or sequence clustering might be more appropriate. The branching-fate framing could still be a neat visualisation.

Ha, fair point, the whole reason we need those tricks is that we destroy the cell when we measure it. With startups you can just follow them over time. I guess the analogy is more like lineage tracing than snapshot inference. Anyway, enough procrastinating, but thanks for humouring me.

Exactly, startups come with their own longitudinal data, closer to live imaging than to a destructive snapshot. Where it could get interesting is founders and employees moving between companies, which creates something like a genealogy of firms, similar to how spinoffs inherit traits from parents. That's been studied in economics as corporate genealogy. But yes, it's more of a thought experiment than a project. Good luck getting back to the real work.

Back to my bone marrow data. I want to pinpoint where multipotent progenitors commit to either the erythroid-megakaryocyte side or the myeloid side. Visually there's a fork in the UMAP but I don't trust UMAP geometry. Is there a statistically grounded way to locate the bifurcation and identify genes that change right at the decision point, rather than just eyeballing a fork?

Yes, avoid relying on UMAP. Options include computing fate probabilities toward each terminal state with tools like CellRank or Palantir, then defining the decision region where fate entropy is highest, meaning cells are still uncommitted, followed by where it drops. Branch-point detection methods in Slingshot-style or graph-based approaches also identify where lineage curves separate. For genes, test for differential expression between branches as a function of position near the split, for example with branch-aware generalised additive models such as those in tradeSeq.

The entropy idea is nice because it's quantitative. My worry is that the commitment point might not be a sharp fork at all, more like a gradual bias that builds up, in which case a 'branch point' is somewhat artificial. And I'd love to check whether the region I find matches where clones in our barcoding experiment start to become restricted to one fate.

Your concern matches current thinking in hematopoiesis, where commitment is often described as a continuum of gradually increasing fate bias rather than discrete forks. You could report the fate probability gradient along the progression rather than a single point, and fit sigmoid curves to estimate where bias crosses a threshold, with confidence intervals by bootstrapping cells. Comparing with your clonal data is a strong test: if early cells whose clones are fate-restricted fall after your inferred decision region, and multipotent clones before it, that supports your localisation independently.
